source: (1) Trevor Stuart (SVP and GM, Harness), 'We're measuring the gains and missing the costs', Harness blog, May 13, 2026 (page shows 'Last updated: 2026-10-09'). Opened: https://www.harness.io/blog/we-re-measuring-the-gains-and-missing-the-costs . (2) Harness press release 'Harness Report Reveals AI Has Outpaced How Engineering Organizations Measure Developer Productivity', San Francisco, May 13, 2026. Opened: https://www.harness.io/press-and-news/ai-has-outpaced-how-engineering-organizations-measure-developer-productivity . (3) The report itself, 'The State of Engineering Excellence 2026: AI Productivity Is Up. The Way We Measure It Is Falling Behind.' (Harness, 10-page PDF), linked from https://www.harness.io/state-of-engineering-excellence . Opened in full: https://cdn.prod.website-files.com/69e786e187c925d08ee02b90/6a3e278e99281bfdec295728_The%20State%20of%20Engineering%20Excellence%20report%202026_letter%20size%20(1).pdf
data_type: Survey (commissioned vendor survey, self-report). No telemetry.
sample_and_method: Press release, 'About the Research': 'This report is based on a survey of 700 software engineering practitioners and managers from large enterprises, commissioned by Harness and conducted by independent research firm Sapio Research in April 2026. The sample included 300 respondents from the United States and 100 each from the United Kingdom, India, France, and Germany.' The report PDF says 'we commissioned a survey of 700 engineering practitioners and their managers from large enterprises across the U.S., U.K., France, Germany, and India' but does not name Sapio or give fieldwork dates. Neither source gives the manager/practitioner split, recruitment method (presumably a panel), company-size threshold, question wording, or margin of error.
vendor_interest: Yes. Harness sells an AI software delivery platform and an engineering-measurement product, Software Engineering Insights (SEI). The blog closes by pitching new SEI capabilities that show 'how much of it is shipping, what the review and validation overhead actually looks like, and where AI spend is producing returns versus producing churn.' The findings point straight at the gap its product claims to fill.
headline_figures: Report PDF: '89% of engineering leaders say productivity metrics have improved since deploying AI.' / '81% say code review time has increased.' / 'When 81% of engineering leaders report that code review time has increased since deploying AI, that's not a footnote to the productivity story. It's a direct offset to it.' / '31% of a developer's day is now consumed by AI-related invisible work that appears in no metric.' / Top sources of AI friction: 'Reviewing AI code for accuracy 53%', 'Fixing subtle bugs from AI code 52%', 'Explaining AI code to teammates 48%', 'Context switching between tools 45%'. / 'the largest source of invisible overhead — reviewing AI-generated code — is only tracked by 38% of organizations.' / '94% say tech debt, validation time, and developer burnout are missing from their current metrics.' / 'And only 6% believe their current frameworks are sufficient to close that gap.' / '15% of Managers have no concerns.' '4% of Practitioners have no concerns.' / '54% fear individual performance evaluations based on AI data.' / Developers prioritise: 55% separating improvement data from performance data, 50% transparency about what is measured, 49% developer involvement in defining metrics. Press release only (not in PDF): '89% of engineering leaders say developer productivity has improved since adopting AI coding tools, and 88% say developer satisfaction has improved.' / '81% say developers spend more time in code review since adopting AI coding tools, with 28% reporting a significant increase of more than 30%.' / '89% say their current metrics accurately reflect AI's impact, yet 94% say key factors, including tech debt, validation time, and developer burnout, are missing from those same metrics.' / biggest challenge: 'measuring true productivity impact (26%), maintaining code quality with AI (24%), and proving ROI to leadership (18%)' (this one is also in the landing page text) / '46% of respondents cite struggling with pressure to work faster than is sustainable, and the same share report privacy or surveillance concerns.' Blog: 'Managers, by contrast, show far greater comfort with these systems: they are nearly four times more likely than developers to report having no concerns at all.'
metric_layer: Mostly input/usage and perceived activity/output (leader-reported productivity and satisfaction), plus self-reported workload overhead (review time, share of day on invisible AI work) and what measurement systems capture. Delivery is discussed as a recommendation ('Know your ship rate') and an anecdote, not measured. Quality appears only as reported friction and as a factor missing from metrics. No financial outcome is measured; the blog's 'a 20% productivity improvement' to show a CFO is a hypothetical, and the report's '20% gain alongside an unmeasured 31% overhead' is an illustration, not a survey result.
respondent_role_split: The only explicit numeric split: no concerns about how AI productivity data might be used to evaluate them, managers 15% vs practitioners 4% (report PDF and press release; blog and press release describe this as 'nearly four times'). The report says 'On every measured dimension, leaders report more favorable conditions than the practitioners actually doing the work', but prints no other split figures. The 89% (productivity improved), 81% (review time up), 89% (metrics accurate) and 94% (factors missing) are attributed to 'engineering leaders' in the blog and PDF, while the press release says simply '89% say' / '81% say', so the base for these is unclear [uncertain]. The 31% figure is attributed to developers in the blog ('developers estimate'), to 'Organizations estimate' in the press release, and stated flatly in the PDF.
workload_signal: 81% say code review time has increased since deploying AI; press release adds 28% report a significant increase of more than 30%. 31% of a developer's day consumed by AI-related invisible work that appears in no metric. Friction: reviewing AI code 53%, fixing subtle bugs from AI code 52%, explaining AI code to teammates 48%, context switching 45%. Press release: 46% cite 'pressure to work faster than is sustainable'. Burnout is named only as a factor 94% say is missing from metrics. Blog gives anecdotes: 'a developer sitting with a pull request for 45 minutes because the AI-generated code is technically correct but written in a style nobody on the team recognizes', and debugging an edge case 'which takes longer to track down than writing the function would have.'
definition_of_value_offered: Partly. It argues for net rather than gross productivity and for shipped value over generated output. Blog: 'Most organizations can tell you how much AI code was accepted. Very few can tell you how much of it actually landed in production, and that's the number that matters.' Report: 'Organizations are measuring gross output. They are not measuring where the productivity gains are actually being spent.' Recommendations (report p.9): measure validation work alongside output (AI review time, debugging overhead, context-switching costs); 'Know your ship rate: Generating more code is not the same as shipping more value... AI increases code volume. It does not automatically increase delivery.'; treat measurement confidence as a risk signal; design for increasing complexity; build trust in first. Press release adds: track 'AI agent accuracy, acceptance, and cost separately from human developer output, with a shared definition of "good" across the organization.' It keeps DORA, cycle time and velocity ('These frameworks remain foundational') and proposes extending them. It does not define a financial ROI method or a threshold for 'paying off'.
removal_counterfactual: None. No data on teams without AI tools or after tool removal; all figures are 'since deploying AI' self-reports.
key_quotes: 1. 'Organizations are measuring gross output. They are not measuring where the productivity gains are actually being spent.' (report PDF, p.4). 2. 'Most organizations can tell you how much AI code was accepted. Very few can tell you how much of it actually landed in production, and that's the number that matters.' (Trevor Stuart, Harness blog, 13 May 2026).
caveats: Vendor-commissioned self-report survey; Harness sells the measurement product the findings argue for. No question wording, no manager/practitioner counts, no margin of error. Figures shift across Harness's own write-ups: the 89% is 'developer productivity has improved' in the blog and press release but 'productivity metrics have improved' in the PDF; the 31% is 'developers estimate' (blog), 'Organizations estimate' (press release) and an unattributed fact in the PDF, and is a perception of time, not measured time. The '89% say their current metrics accurately reflect AI's impact' figure appears in the blog and press release but not in the PDF. The 6% is 'think they're equipped to close them' (blog), 'believe the frameworks they have today can fix it' (press release), and 'believe their current frameworks are sufficient to close that gap' (PDF). The 20% productivity gain is illustrative, not a finding. The 89% and 94% coexisting may reflect different question framings rather than contradictory beliefs by the same people. Sample is large enterprises in five countries only.
access: Opened in full: the blog, the press release, and the 10-page report PDF (extracted with pdftotext). Not verified: question wording, role counts, and whether the 89%/81%/94% bases are leaders only or all 700 respondents (the press release and PDF/blog disagree in phrasing); the press-release-only figures (88%, 28%, 46%, 89% metrics accurate) are not in the PDF and rely on Harness's press release; no separate methodology appendix from Sapio Research was found.
